meetings.headline: Town meeting reversed a failed vote to pay Fitchburg the water bills Lunenburg forgot to send for over a year
meetings.summary: This special town meeting worked through 17+ warrant articles, most contentiously a near-failed then reconsidered vote to pay Fitchburg for water bills the town had failed to send to 11 accounts for over a year, plus a $195,790.97 FY26 budget amendment driven by heavy finance-department staff turnover. Town meeting also funded a storm water utility consultant and a capital cost-estimating fund, created a special education out-of-district reserve fund, raised the senior tax-deferral income limit, adopted an MBTA Communities Act zoning overlay at Tritown, revised SAP personnel/benefit rules, passed over a Kids Kingdom playground transfer and a warrant-mailing change amid public pushback, and narrowly voted down eliminating the town's volunteer personnel committee.

minutes.headline: Town meeting reversed a failed vote to pay Fitchburg the water bills Lunenburg forgot to send for over a year
minutes.summary: This special town meeting worked through 17+ warrant articles, most contentiously a near-failed then reconsidered vote to pay Fitchburg for water bills the town had failed to send to 11 accounts for over a year, plus a $195,790.97 FY26 budget amendment driven by heavy finance-department staff turnover. Town meeting also funded a storm water utility consultant and a capital cost-estimating fund, created a special education out-of-district reserve fund, raised the senior tax-deferral income limit, adopted an MBTA Communities Act zoning overlay at Tritown, revised SAP personnel/benefit rules, passed over a Kids Kingdom playground transfer and a warrant-mailing change amid public pushback, and narrowly voted down eliminating the town's volunteer personnel committee.

what_happened.line: Town meeting rejected, then reconsidered and passed, paying Fitchburg for water bills the town failed to send to 11 accounts for over a year.
Town meeting approved a mid-year FY26 budget amendment driven by turnover of the finance director, assistant accountant, and payroll coordinator.
Town meeting created a special education out-of-district reserve fund over the finance committee's own recommendation against it.
Town meeting adopted a zoning overlay at Tritown to comply with the state's MBTA Communities Act.
Town meeting narrowly voted to keep the volunteer personnel committee rather than dissolve it.

why_it_matters: The Fitchburg billing lapse left the water enterprise fund short of budgeted revenue, which the finance director said could complicate setting the tax rate, and it is the reason a related capital-fund transfer needed town meeting approval at all.

The new special education reserve fund is a standing account town meeting still controls dollar by dollar, meant to absorb the swings in out-of-district placement costs that have come up in three straight budget seasons.
The MBTA Communities zoning overlay is a compliance vote, not a building proposal by itself, but it sets the multifamily density allowed at Tritown going forward.
watch_next: The storm water task force said it plans to bring a storm water utility article to the spring 2026 annual town meeting.
Whether the water enterprise fund needs a rate adjustment or further transfer to cover the billing shortfall.

meetings.headline: Voters rejected both the $13.8M Marshall Park and $22.4M municipal building debt exclusions; a school override petition narrowly passed
meetings.summary: This was Lunenburg's 2025 Annual Town Meeting, covering the FY26 omnibus budget (~$49.4M, passed), a full capital plan, and two major debt-exclusion building projects. Voters approved the FY26 budget and a citizen-petitioned contingent school override appropriation by a narrow margin, but rejected both the Marshall Park renovation and the municipal building design (new town hall/Ritter/meeting house) debt exclusions, each falling short of the required two-thirds supermajority after extended public debate. A separate citizen petition seeking town-meeting oversight of the cemetery commission's powers was also defeated as a non-binding advisory question.

The town's overall FY26 budget motion, raised via taxation and multiple enterprise/revolving fund transfers.
Property taxes are the largest funding source at roughly 72% of available funds; net state aid is about 20%; local receipts make up the next largest share.
Health insurance costs rose 14.84% this year through the MIIA trust, a steeper jump than the 5-7% increases of recent years, and is expected to continue trending upward.
Total education budget covers Lunenburg Public Schools and the Monty Tech assessment; the school budget rose about 3.64% over FY25's post-override total and Monty Tech's assessment rose 8.88%.
Last year's $50,000 grant-writer funding went unused; it is now funded outside the operating budget as a pilot via free cash, expected to be used partly by the parks commission.

The petition sought to appropriate a sum equal to the school department's level-service funding gap, contingent on a future Prop 2½ ballot override; the proponent said this year's gap is about $2 million versus last year's roughly $948,000.

A debt-exclusion request to renovate Marshall Park; a reduced-scope alternative was also costed out; the parks commission had returned $1.5 million in state grants it could not match in time.

A debt-exclusion request to renovate the meeting house and Ritter building and build a new town hall, consolidating town and school district offices; the town has spent $937,000 in capital funds over seven years maintaining the current buildings.
The citizen petitioner argued the cemetery commission holds substantial sale-of-lots and perpetual-care funds that were not tapped before the commission sought $50,000 in tax-funded capital money.

minutes.headline: Voters rejected both the $13.8M Marshall Park and $22.4M municipal building debt exclusions; a school override petition narrowly passed
minutes.summary: This was Lunenburg's 2025 Annual Town Meeting, covering the FY26 omnibus budget (~$49.4M, passed), a full capital plan, and two major debt-exclusion building projects. Voters approved the FY26 budget and a citizen-petitioned contingent school override appropriation by a narrow margin, but rejected both the Marshall Park renovation and the municipal building design (new town hall/Ritter/meeting house) debt exclusions, each falling short of the required two-thirds supermajority after extended public debate. A separate citizen petition seeking town-meeting oversight of the cemetery commission's powers was also defeated as a non-binding advisory question.

watch_next: Select board scheduling the Proposition 2½ override ballot vote ahead of the extended November 15, 2025 contingency deadline
Whether the Marshall Park or municipal building projects return on a future town meeting warrant

what_happened.line: Voters rejected the Marshall Park debt exclusion, short of the two-thirds majority a debt exclusion requires.
Voters also rejected a debt exclusion for the municipal building project covering the meeting house, Ritter and a new town hall.
A citizen-petitioned school override appropriation passed by a narrow margin.
The FY26 town operating budget passed.
A related free cash transfer to schools, contingent on the override outcome, passed, and its contingency deadline was later pushed to November.

why_it_matters: Rejecting both debt exclusions means neither the park renovation nor the town hall/Ritter/meeting house project is funded for now, and either would have added to property tax bills had it passed.
The override's narrow passage moves a Proposition 2½ question toward a separate town-wide ballot; residents would still have to approve it there for it to add school funding outside the levy cap.
The FY26 budget's passage keeps town and school departments funded for the coming fiscal year regardless of the override outcome.
